newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. INFLATION JITTERS HOLD OLOS IN THEIR GRIP.
newsitem.headline: U.S. INFLATION JITTERS HOLD OLOS IN THEIR GRIP.

text.p: Belgian bond futures advanced on Wednesday, but dealers said trade was thin and many were nervous about upcoming U.S. inflation data.

"The slightest sign of a pick-up in inflation in the U.S. and German, and Belgian yields, will shoot higher," said a trader. The jump could be in excess of a quarter of a point, the level by which the U.S. Fed is expected to raise U.S. interest rates if inflation does trend higher.
"A 25 basis point rate rise in the U.S. is already discounted," the trader said. Before the inflation data the market would be eyeing the Federal Reserve's Beige Book.
The Beige Book, due at 1600 GMT, would be examined carefully for signs that the Fed was finding evidence of more wage pressure and/or price pressure, dealers said.
After that the fate of the market would be tied to U.S. producer price data due on Thursday and CPI numbers on Friday, both for August.
While CPI is forecast to have remained steady, the market might suffer an upset from the PPI data which are expected to point to a mild increase in inflation further down the pipeline.
"Anything like plus 0.2 percent (month-on-month) on PPI would send the market into a tailspin," a trader said.
Meanwhile the market benefitted from a continued short squeeze and technical strength for Bunds.
September bond futures were up 23 basis points at 117.25 and usually lacklustre futures on three-month interbank francs gained one basis point at 96.82.
But in the cash market the benchmark 10-year OLO yielded 6.55 percent, unchanged from Tuesday, and the spread over Bunds was steady at 24 basis points.
The franc recovered partly from the pressure from concern about the political fallout from allegations of judicial bungling in criminal scandals rocking Belgium.
The franc was at 20.5980/95 to the mark at 1555 GMT, up from 20.6005/15 late on Tuesday. Dealers noted the concern had been limited to the currency and money markets, though.
